checks.invariant: audit retention runs only through the 03:00 scheduled job, and the purge function is not callable by lower-privilege or anonymous roles

No migration revokes execute from public or grants it narrowly for this function — the only revoke/grant pairs in the whole migrations tree are set_jadwal_token (20261016000001:74-75) and reset_jadwal (20261016000002:28-29) — so the Postgres default EXECUTE-to-PUBLIC grant stands and any PostgREST caller (anon or any authenticated account) can trigger the delete via RPC. supabase/all_in_one_setup.sql repeats the same un-revoked definition (1201-1217). The repo's own DB suite skips this file entirely (*audit_log_retention* in check-prodi-db.sh:20, pg_cron absent in Docker), so no existing test asserts the function's privileges. Linked fingerprint: audit-log/purge_old_audit_log/public-execute.

candidates.title: audit_log purge function is executable by any PostgREST caller, turning the documented nightly-only, append-only retention into an on-demand deletion
candidates.description: purge_old_audit_log() is created as a security-definer function in the public schema and never revoked from PUBLIC in any migration, so the Postgres default EXECUTE grant lets the anon and authenticated API roles invoke it through PostgREST RPC (POST /rest/v1/rpc/purge_old_audit_log). The function deletes every audit_log row older than one month with the owner's rights, so a lower-privilege or even unauthenticated caller can delete audit history ahead of the 03:00 schedule, contradicting both the append-only invariant ('nobody can edit or delete entries') and the documented retention design (nightly pg_cron only).
candidates.claimed_root_cause: The 20260924000007 migration installs the purge function without any privilege control: unlike its siblings set_jadwal_token (20261016000001:74-75) and reset_jadwal (20261016000002:28-29), it neither revokes execute from public nor grants it narrowly, so Postgres leaves the default EXECUTE-to-PUBLIC in place; security definer + set search_path = public then runs the delete with owner rights, bypassing audit_log's select-only RLS and grants.

trace.description: create or replace function purge_old_audit_log() with no revoke from public and no narrow grant; Postgres default EXECUTE to PUBLIC makes it callable by anon and authenticated PostgREST clients.
security definer + set search_path = public executes the body with the migration owner's privileges, bypassing RLS and the select-only grant on audit_log.
The same function is what the nightly 03:00 cron job invokes, confirming the intended invocation channel is scheduler-only, not RPC.
delete from audit_log where at < now() - interval '1 month' — a caller-triggered invocation removes audit rows ahead of the night's schedule and outside any role gate.

evidence.description: Function definition; the file ends at the cron.schedule call with no accompanying revoke/grant.
Sibling security-definer function explicitly revokes execute from public (line 74) and grants only to authenticated (line 75) — the control missing on the purge function.
Second sibling (reset_jadwal) repeats the revoke-from-public / grant-to-authenticated pattern (28-29).
Comment: no insert/update/delete policy for authenticated on purpose, the log is append-only for everyone else — an exposed delete function contradicts this invariant.
Documented design: 'Nightly pg_cron job purges entries older than 1 month' (also 645: retention is a nightly pg_cron purge).
The one-shot setup script embeds the same un-revoked definition (1201-1217).
The repo's Docker DB suite skips *audit_log_retention*, so no existing test asserts the function's privileges.

blockers: No OS-enforced sandbox on this host (no network isolation, empty-environment guarantee, read-only mounts or resource limits): no target code, PostgREST or local Postgres may be started, so has_function_privilege() and an actual anon-role invocation could not be observed.

Even the repo's own Docker harness skips the retention migration (*audit_log_retention* in check-prodi-db.sh:20) because pg_cron does not exist in plain Postgres; a local confirmation needs a cron-schema stub.

Whether the migration is applied as-is on the deployed project and whether PostgREST RPC exposure of the public schema is enabled are deployment facts not visible in the repository (no supabase/config.toml).

validation_plan.local: In the required OS sandbox: start a throwaway Postgres 16, apply scripts/db-stub.sql, create a minimal cron stub (no-op cron.schedule/unschedule), apply 20260924000007_audit_log_retention.sql, then assert has_function_privilege('anon','public.purge_old_audit_log()','EXECUTE') and has_function_privilege('authenticated', ...); insert two dummy audit_log rows (one older, one newer than 1 month), set an anon request context with no sub claim, call the function, and verify only the older row is deleted.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed on a controlled project: in the Supabase SQL editor run select proacl from pg_proc where proname='purge_old_audit_log' (null proacl means default PUBLIC EXECUTE → issue present) or has_function_privilege('anon','public.purge_old_audit_log()','EXECUTE'), and confirm whether a revoke/grant migration has been applied.

candidates.title: User-management changes written through the service-role client are logged with a null actor and read as 'Sistem', defeating who-changed-what attribution
candidates.description: SUPERADMIN user management (create user, change role, change prodi access, delete user) executes through createAdminClient(), whose requests carry the service key instead of a user session. The audit_row() trigger derives the actor from auth.uid(), which is null on those requests, so the resulting audit_log rows for the most privilege-sensitive changes (role grants/revocations) store actor_id and actor_email as null and render as 'Sistem', even though the audit log is documented to record who changed what.
candidates.claimed_root_cause: The audit trigger derives the actor solely from auth.uid() (20260924000005:53, redefined at 20261008000003:33), while the pengguna actions perform profiles writes with the service-role client (pengguna/actions.ts:54, 62, 81, 86, 102, 103, 119, 124), whose JWT has no sub — so the trigger stores null actor for exactly the operations an audit log exists to attribute, and the UI then labels them 'Sistem'.

trace.description: updateUserRoleAction (behind requireSuperadmin) updates profiles.role through the admin client; the same pattern covers create (62), prodi access (103) and delete (124).
createAdminClient() sends SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY; the request carries no authenticated user session, so no user subject reaches the database session.
actor := auth.uid() — null for service-role requests (same pattern as 20260924000005:53).
insert into audit_log (actor_id, actor_email, ...) values (null, null, ...) — the row becomes unattributed and the UI renders null actor as 'Sistem' (riwayat/page.tsx:72, 139).

evidence.description: Account creation uses the admin client (auth.admin.createUser, 55), and the resulting profiles insert arrives via handle_new_user with no JWT at all.
Role grant/revoke update written with the admin client.
Service-role client construction — the only credential on these requests is the service key.
actor uuid := auth.uid() in the trigger.
Header states the log records 'who changed what' — attribution is the documented purpose.
Design doc: 'It records actor (from auth.uid()), action, table, record id...' (also 361: the browser filters by actor).
The UI displays row.actor_email ?? 'Sistem' — unattributed rows read as an anonymous system actor (also the actor count at 72).
Contrast: LOGIN/LOGOUT rows pass actor_id/actor_email explicitly, so the gap is specific to data-table writes executed with the service role.

blockers: No OS-enforced sandbox on this host: a database (or PostgREST/GoTrue stack) cannot be started to execute a service-role profiles update and read back the resulting audit row.

The decisive comparison needs the Supabase auth semantics (auth.uid() over a service JWT with no sub); the repo stub models only request.jwt.claim.sub, so the local check must reproduce the no-subject context faithfully.
No source-visible wrapper adds actor context around createAdminClient; confirming no deployment-level hook does so requires owner observation.

validation_plan.local: In the required OS sandbox: reuse the repo's harness pattern (scripts/db-stub.sql + migrations) on a throwaway Postgres; insert a dummy profiles row, then set role service_role with request.jwt.claim.sub='' (no subject) and update the profiles row; assert the new audit_log row has actor_id IS NULL and actor_email IS NULL, while the same update under set_config('request.jwt.claim.sub', <dummy uuid>) records that actor.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed on a staging project: change one dummy account's role through /pengguna as SUPERADMIN, then open Log Aktivitas → Riwayat for table profiles and confirm whether the new row shows 'Sistem' instead of the SUPERADMIN's email.

candidates.title: Full audit-log read is granted to every authenticated account while account creation depends on an unpinned provider signup setting
candidates.description: audit_log's only policy grants SELECT with using (true) to the authenticated role, and any account — including one created through the provider's signup endpoint — receives a VIEWER profile automatically and lands on that same authenticated tier. If the Supabase project allows new-user signup (a dashboard setting the repository does not pin), any internet user holding the public anon key can mint a session and read the entire audit history — actor emails, before/after snapshots of schedules, settings and user management — through PostgREST or /log-aktivitas, contradicting the staff-only assumption the open-read policy relies on.
candidates.claimed_root_cause: The staff-only assumption behind audit_log_select_authenticated (using (true)) has no source-level enforcement: handle_new_user() creates a VIEWER profile for any auth.users row, and the repository contains no supabase/config.toml, allowed-domain rule, or app-side signup that pins who may create accounts — the signup gate lives only in the Supabase dashboard, outside source control.

trace.description: handle_new_user() inserts a profiles row with role 'VIEWER' for every new auth.users row; the provider's signup endpoint (project setting external to the repo) is the account source.
The after-insert trigger on auth.users makes the VIEWER provisioning automatic for any account-creation path.
The page queries audit_log with the session client and applies no role check, so any authenticated session reaches the full log UI.
using (true) for the authenticated role returns every audit row (all actors, all before/after snapshots) to that account via PostgREST or the UI.

evidence.description: profiles.role defaults to 'VIEWER' — the least privileged role, but still authenticated-tier access.
The select policy body: using (true), scoped only by the authenticated role.
'There is no sign-up page' — a UI statement only; the provider-level signup setting is not recorded anywhere in the repo (no supabase/config.toml exists).
select('*') against audit_log with the session client, no role gate.
Per-record history view selects full snapshots ('*') from audit_log for the same audience, exposing values meant for staff eyes (settings, user emails, thesis titles in defenses snapshots).

blockers: The decisive fact is provider-side: the Supabase Auth 'Allow new users to sign up' (and email-confirmation) setting of the deployed project; no supabase/config.toml exists to pin it and the hosted project cannot be inspected in this run.
No OS-enforced sandbox on this host: a local Supabase/PostgREST stack cannot be started to demonstrate signup → VIEWER profile → full audit_log read.
Whether POST /auth/v1/signup (or another enabled provider) is reachable on the deployed project is deployment state not visible in the repository.

validation_plan.local: In the required OS sandbox: apply the migrations on the stub Postgres, insert a dummy auth.users row with no prior profile (simulating the signup trigger), then set role authenticated with that new user's sub and query audit_log and profiles to show the new account gets role VIEWER and can read every audit row in the table.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed on the deployed project: record the Supabase dashboard state at Authentication → Sign In / Providers → Email ('Allow new users to sign up'); if enabled, verify on a controlled staging project (then delete the test account) that POST /auth/v1/signup with the public anon key yields a session that can load /log-aktivitas; if disabled, this candidate collapses into the general provisioning uncovered item.

hardening: supabase/README.md:9 promises all_in_one_setup.sql is 'Every migration in migrations/, joined in order', but the copy stops at 20261017000002_wakil_dekan_semua_jadwal: 20261012000001_sessions_jenis_kelas (sessions jenis_kelas split), 20261017000003_defense_link (defenses.link + http(s) enforcement) and 20261017000004_hari_libur (holidays table) are missing — a fresh one-shot setup loses those features (and the holidays warnings) while every security control (roles, RLS, audit log, retention, grants) is present. The same README (line 61) still describes the obsolete USING(true) WITH CHECK(true) policy model.

A gitlink .claude/worktrees/perf-and-features (mode 160000) is tracked without any .gitmodules entry: a stray submodule reference to a local workspace that breaks submodule tooling on fresh clones and is not covered by .gitignore — remove it or ignore the path.

next.config.ts configures no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors, X-Content-Type-Options or HSTS headers; only the jadwal-dosen noindex/referrer header pair exists (29-39). Add baseline security headers at the config or edge layer.

createAdminClient() falls back to https://placeholder.supabase.co when NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL is unset while the real service key is present (admin.ts:10-11), so a misconfigured deploy would send the credential to the provider's default host instead of failing closed; make the URL required like the service key.

The repo's DB suite skips the retention migration (check-prodi-db.sh:20, pg_cron absent in Docker) and check:audit-log only tests pure filter/formatting helpers, so purge_old_audit_log's existence, schedule and privileges are never asserted; add a cron-stubbed apply with has_function_privilege assertions.

Dependencies are pinned via package-lock.json and installed with npm ci, but no offline advisory data was available in this run to check next 16.3.8, @supabase/supabase-js, @supabase/ssr, exceljs and docx against known CVEs; run an advisory scan as a networked maintenance check.

Provenance note: repository HEAD moved from the run-pinned f721504 to 3ca6a4f during this review; the only tracked delta is UI copy in the peer-owned src/app/jadwal-dosen/[token]/page.tsx, so every path reviewed by this hunter is byte-identical across both revisions.

uncovered.surface: authenticated-principal provisioning (who may become an authenticated account)
uncovered.boundary: the tier that every 'to authenticated using (true)' SELECT policy trusts across all data tables
uncovered.reason: Every data-table read policy is 'using (true)' to authenticated and depends on the undocumented, unenforced assumption that only staff hold accounts, while handle_new_user auto-provisions VIEWER for any auth.users row and account creation is controlled by the provider's signup setting (no supabase/config.toml in the repo). The audit-log-scoped effect is only candidate audit-log/select-authenticated/public-signup-exposure in unit 2; the repository-wide variant (schedules, lecturers, student names/thesis titles, settings, profiles) has no coverage unit and needs one deterministic unit that pins the provisioning path.
